scenes.heading: Planning a synthesis
scenes.sub: Start at the target and work backwards
scenes.say: Every medicine made in a factory comes from a planned synthesis. Chemists don't guess forwards. They work backwards from the target molecule, using the reactions they know as tools.

scenes.heading: Think of it like this
scenes.everyday: Working out a recipe from a dish you tasted at a restaurant
scenes.science: Retrosynthesis: what could this target be made from?
scenes.breaks: you can guess when cooking, but every disconnection must match a real reaction, and synthons like R⁻ never exist on their own.
scenes.say: Retrosynthesis is like tasting a great dish and working out the recipe. You work backwards: this sauce is probably tomatoes and garlic, which you can buy. In chemistry, you make imaginary disconnections, and ask what each piece could be made from, until you reach cheap starting materials.

scenes.heading: Good disconnections
points: Break bonds next to functional groups
Split near the middle: similar-sized pieces
Count carbons: need a C–C bond step?
scenes.say: Disconnect next to a functional group, near the middle of the molecule. Count carbons first. If the target has more than your starting material, you need a C C bond-forming step, like cyanide, which adds one carbon, or a Grignard reagent.
scenes.caption: Disconnect next to a functional group, near the middle of the molecule. Count carbons first. If the target has more than your starting material, you need a C–C bond-forming step, like cyanide, which adds one carbon, or a Grignard reagent.

scenes.heading: Worked example: two steps
scenes.question: Make propanoic acid from 10.0 g of bromoethane. Step yields: 85% and 75%.
scenes.say: Propanoic acid has three carbons, bromoethane has two, so add one with cyanide. Then hydrolyse the nitrile to the acid. Yields multiply as decimals: zero point eight five times zero point seven five is about sixty-four percent. From ten grams, you get four point three three grams of acid.
scenes.caption: Propanoic acid has three carbons, bromoethane has two, so add one with cyanide. Then hydrolyse the nitrile to the acid. Yields multiply as decimals: 0.85 × 0.75 ≈ 64%. From 10.0 g, you get 4.33 g of acid.

scenes.heading: Protecting groups
scenes.say: Sometimes a reagent would attack the wrong group. Then use a protecting group, like masking tape when you paint. Turn the ketone into a cyclic acetal, reduce the ester with lithium aluminium hydride, then peel the tape off with aqueous acid.

scenes.heading: Linear vs convergent
scenes.say: Six steps at ninety percent each give only fifty-three percent overall. A little spills at every step. A convergent synthesis makes fragments in parallel, like splitting up a group assignment, so less is wasted.
scenes.caption: Six steps at 90% each give only 53% overall. A little spills at every step. A convergent synthesis makes fragments in parallel, like splitting up a group assignment, so less is wasted.

scenes.say: Quick recap. Work backwards from the target. Disconnect next to functional groups. Keep Grignards dry. Protect a group only when you must, because it adds two steps. And yields multiply. Now try the practice questions!
